I submitted two planets. The first is clearly detected; the second is weak, and the BIC slightly favours the one-planet model.

| | Planet 1 | Planet 2 (weak) |
|---|---|---|
| Period (days) | 278.27 | 11.205 |
| Velocity amplitude, K (m/s) | about 29.7 | about 0.42 |
| Minimum mass (Jupiter masses) | 0.942 | 0.0045 (about 1.4 Earth masses) |
| Eccentricity | 0.068 | 0.15 |
| omega (rad) | 3.856 | 1.793 |
| l (rad) | 5.109 | 2.978 |

Jitter was set to 0.1 m/s, the minimum allowed. The leftover scatter after fitting (0.42 m/s) is already below the median measurement error (0.56 m/s), so no extra noise term was needed.

- **The 278-day planet:** It is the dominant periodogram peak. Fitting it alone brings the scatter down from 19.4 m/s to 0.50 m/s.
- **The 11.2-day planet:** It is the strongest peak left after removing the first planet. Fitting it lowers chi-squared from 65.0 to 45.9 and the scatter to 0.42 m/s. That improvement is smaller than the BIC penalty for the five extra parameters, so the BIC went from 144.8 to 148.2. I kept it because of a shuffle test: in 100 random reshuffles of the leftover data, the 99th-percentile peak was 2.68 and the real peak is 2.72, a false-alarm chance of roughly 1%. With only 100 reshuffles that estimate is rough. Its 0.15 eccentricity is also poorly constrained at this amplitude.

If the 11.2-day signal is noise, this submission includes one spurious planet. The one-planet alternative was the 278-day orbit by itself, with slightly different fitted values (P = 278.22 days, e = 0.066).
